o: Process transactions left to right, keeping a running balance that must never dip below 0; you may skip transactions. In [2,-5,3,-1,-2] taking everything dips to -3, but dropping -5 yields 4 transactions. In [-1,-2,-3] nothing can be taken. The tag hint (greedy + heap) suggests an exchange argument: whenever the balance would go negative after accepting a transaction, undo the single most harmful (most negative) accepted transaction so far.
k: Accept greedily; if balance < 0, remove the most negative accepted value via a min-heap.
Each removal restores validity and drops exactly one transaction, keeping the count maximal.

a.n: Greedy with Min-Heap of Accepted Negatives
a.i: Maintain balance and a min-heap of all accepted transaction values. Accept every transaction; if the balance turns negative, pop the smallest (most negative) value from the heap and add it back to the balance. An exchange argument shows replacing the currently most damaging acceptance with a skip is always at least as good, so the final heap size is the maximum feasible count.
s: For each transaction t: add t to balance, push t, increment count.
If balance < 0: pop the minimum v, set balance -= v, decrement count.

c.python:
import heapq
class Solution:
    def maxTransactions(self, transactions):
        bal = 0
        cnt = 0
        h = []
        for t in transactions:
            bal += t
            heapq.heappush(h, t)
            cnt += 1
            if bal < 0:
                bal -= heapq.heappop(h)
                cnt -= 1
        return cnt

a.t: O(n log n) — each element pushed and popped at most once

w: Use 64-bit balances since values reach 1e9 and n reaches 1e5. Pitfall: popping the largest positive instead of the most negative — the fix must maximize the restored balance. Follow-up: return which transactions were skipped, or handle a nonzero starting balance.
